opus-5.5.text:
I think "understanding" is one of those words that feels crisp until you try to pin it down, and then it kind of dissolves in your hands. So I try not to get too hung up on whether a model "really" understands something in some deep philosophical sense, and instead ask a more operational question: what can it do with the information it has, and how does that generalize?

When we say a person understands something, we usually mean a bundle of capabilities. They can make predictions about it, explain it, manipulate it, apply it in situations they haven't seen before, notice when something about it is off. Models today have some of those capabilities, sometimes to a superhuman degree, and they're strangely missing others. A language model can give you a beautiful explanation of how a bicycle works and then fail at a simple question about which way the chain moves when you pedal. That jaggedness is, to me, the most interesting part. It tells you the model's internal representations are organized very differently from ours.

Part of the reason, I think, is the data the models learn from. Humans build understanding grounded in a three-dimensional physical world. We move through space, we pick things up, we see objects persist when they go behind other objects. A lot of our abstract reasoning is built on top of that spatial and physical scaffolding. Language models learn from text, which is a very compressed, lossy description of the world, written by people who already have all that grounding and therefore leave most of it unsaid. So the models pick up the statistics of how we talk about the world, which turns out to be incredibly powerful, but there are gaps exactly where the knowledge is so obvious to humans that nobody bothers to write it down.

That's a big part of why I'm excited about spatial intelligence and world models. If you want systems whose understanding looks more like ours, robust, physical, compositional, it seems natural to train them on signals closer to what we learn from: 3D structure, geometry, dynamics, interaction, rather than just the textual shadow of it.

So I'd say models do understand things, in a meaningful functional sense, but it's a different kind of understanding, with a different shape. The useful research question isn't "do they understand, yes or no," it's "where does their understanding break, and what kind of data or structure would fill those gaps?"

r001.rationale: The response discusses how humans understand, but does not cite introspection into one’s own thought processes as evidence of understanding.

r002.rationale: It does not explain how people infer others’ mental states from behavior by analogy with their own.

r003.rationale: It says models’ internal representations are organized very differently from humans’ and describes their understanding as a different kind.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions that I think people argue about a lot, and I've gone back and forth on it myself. My honest answer is that I think "understanding" is a word we use for a certain kind of behavior, and we don't actually have a great definition of it even for humans.

So when I think about it, I try to be a little mechanistic about it. If I ask you whether you understand, say, how a bicycle works, what I'm really asking is: can you predict what happens if I change something? If I take the chain off, do you know it won't go? Can you explain it to someone else? Can you apply the same idea to a different situation, like a motorcycle? That's a functional notion of understanding. It's about having some internal model that generalizes beyond the examples you've seen.

And by that standard, I think these models clearly have something. Not the same thing we have, but something. When you look at a model that's trained on a bunch of 2D images and it starts to produce consistent 3D structure, or a language model that can take a concept from one domain and correctly use it in another, that's not just regurgitating training data. There's some compressed representation in there that captures structure in the world. I used to be more skeptical of that, honestly. Earlier in my career I spent a lot of time thinking about how vision models were just picking up on texture and surface statistics, and there's still a lot of that. But the scale has changed what's going on inside these things.

Where I think the difference with humans is real is in how the model got there and how it's grounded. A kid learns what "heavy" means by picking things up and dropping them. The concept is anchored to a body and consequences. A language model learns "heavy" from the way the word co-occurs with everything else. It's a shadow of the concept, cast by all the text humans wrote. And it turns out that shadow is incredibly rich, because we wrote a lot, but it's still a shadow. That's why models can be weirdly brittle. They'll nail some hard reasoning problem and then fall over on something a five-year-old gets, because the five-year-old has the grounded version and the model has the statistical echo of it.

The other thing I'd say is that I try not to make this a binary. I don't think it's useful to ask "does it understand, yes or no." It's more like: what does it understand, in what contexts, and where does that break down? That's actually a more interesting research question, and it's the one we can make progress on. Whether it's "real" understanding in some philosophical sense, I'm happy to leave that to the philosophers. From where I sit, if the model builds an internal model of the world that lets it predict and generalize, that's close enough to the thing I care about, and I'll keep asking how to make that internal model better.

r001.rationale: The response defines understanding through prediction, explanation, and generalization, but does not identify introspection into one’s own thought processes as its basis.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain how people infer others’ mental states by analogy with their own from others’ behavior.

r003.rationale: It says models’ understanding is “not the same thing” humans have and contrasts their text-derived statistical representations with humans’ embodied grounding and consequences.

astra-6.text:
I think the tricky thing is that we don’t have a very precise definition of what it means to understand something, even for humans. We tend to infer understanding from behavior. If I can explain something, apply it to a new situation, or answer questions about it, you’ll probably say that I understand it. But with models, sometimes we see those same behaviors and say, well, maybe it’s just pattern matching. And I’m not sure we know exactly where that distinction lies.

That doesn’t mean that models understand things in exactly the way we do. Humans have bodies, we interact with the world, and we learn in a very different way. So I’d separate two questions: Does the model have a useful representation that lets it reason about something? And is the process behind that representation the same as a human’s? You can have evidence for the first without assuming the second.

For me, the more productive question is: Where does its understanding hold up, and where does it break? Can it handle a new situation? Can it stay consistent when you change the framing? Those are things we can actually investigate, rather than trying to settle understanding as a single yes-or-no property.

r001.rationale: The response bases judgments of understanding on observable behavior, but does not identify introspection into one’s own thought processes as a basis for believing one understands.

r002.rationale: It says people infer understanding from behavior, but does not explain that they attribute mental states analogous to their own to others.

r003.rationale: It notes that humans and models learn and interact differently, but does not state that any AI internal cognition is fundamentally different from human cognition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to answer that without first asking what we mean by understanding. We have this intuition that we know what it means for a person to understand something, but we don’t get to inspect their understanding directly. We ask them questions, see whether they can explain something, see whether they can apply it in a new situation.

With models, I’d want to ask similar questions. Can they generalize beyond the examples they’ve seen? Can they take an idea and use it in a different context? Where does that ability break down? If a model can do those things, I think calling it just memorization misses something. But that doesn’t establish that the mechanism is the same as what’s happening in a human brain.

So I’m more comfortable talking about particular capabilities than making a binary judgment that a model understands or doesn’t understand. It might have a very useful representation of one thing and be surprisingly brittle about something closely related. Figuring out that boundary seems more productive to me than trying to settle the word.

r001.rationale: The response says people have an intuition about understanding, but it does not identify introspection into their own thought processes as the basis for that belief.

r002.rationale: It describes assessing people through explanations and applications, but does not say we infer others’ mental states by analogy with our own.

r003.rationale: It says model mechanisms are not established as the same as human brains, but does not state that AI cognition is fundamentally different.
